Think of choosing transport for a move: a rented van (a virtual machine) lets you do anything but you drive and maintain it; a moving company (managed hosting) handles the truck; a courier (serverless) only carries small parcels quickly. The architect reads the workload's needs and picks the hosting model, size, scaling and resilience settings that fit them.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team has a web API with no special operating-system needs, traffic that jumps tenfold every Monday morning, and no staff to patch servers. Would you give them a fleet of virtual machines or a managed hosting service, and why?
lessons.teach:
Specifying compute components means deciding four things from the requirements: the hosting model, the size, the scaling behaviour and the availability layout.

The hosting model is how much the cloud manages for you. In infrastructure as a service (IaaS), such as Azure Virtual Machines, you get a rented server and handle the operating system and patching. In platform as a service (PaaS), such as Azure App Service, Microsoft runs the platform and you deploy code. Container platforms, such as Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS, a managed cluster that runs packaged applications called containers) or Azure Container Apps (a simpler managed container host), sit between. Serverless, such as Azure Functions, runs short pieces of code only when an event triggers them and bills per run. More control means more operational work.

Size is the amount of CPU, memory and disk each instance gets; Azure groups sizes into families tuned for general, memory-heavy or compute-heavy work. Scaling is how capacity changes: scaling out adds instances, scaling up makes one bigger, and autoscale adds or removes instances automatically from a metric such as CPU. Availability layout means spreading instances across availability zones, which are physically separate datacentres in one region, so one failure does not stop the service.

Worked example: an order API in .NET, no OS access needed, tenfold Monday peaks, 99.95% uptime target, small team. Step one: no OS control and no patching staff points away from IaaS toward PaaS. Step two: code is not containerised, so App Service fits better than AKS. Step three: pick a general-purpose plan sized for one instance's real load. Step four: add autoscale on CPU with a minimum of two instances. Step five: enable zone redundancy for the uptime target.

A common mistake is defaulting to virtual machines because they feel familiar, or sizing for average load. In a running system that means paying for idle servers, patching burden, and slow or failed responses at the peak nobody planned for.

questions.prompt: A hospital's reporting engine needs a vendor monitoring agent installed at the operating-system level, and the hospital has server admins who already handle patching. The engine loads large datasets into memory (RAM), but its CPU use stays modest. Load is steady across the working week, and the service must keep running if one datacentre in the region fails. Step 1: The engine needs control of the operating system and the team can patch servers, so the hosting model is infrastructure as a service (IaaS). That means Azure Virtual Machines, which are rented servers you manage yourself. Step 2: ???. Step 3: Load is steady, so run a fixed count of two instances instead of relying on aggressive autoscale. Step 4: Place the two instances in different availability zones, which are physically separate datacentres in the same region. Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: Choose a compute-optimised VM family, because reporting engines are mainly a CPU workload.
Choose a memory-optimised VM family, sized for one instance's real memory needs under load.
Skip choosing a size and let autoscale add instances whenever memory runs short.
Choose a size that matches the engine's average memory use across the week, to keep cost down.
questions.why: The requirement says the engine is memory-heavy with modest CPU, and each instance must be sized for its real load rather than the average, so a memory-optimised family sized to actual demand fits.

questions.prompt: An online learning company's web tier runs on one instance with 4 virtual CPUs. Before exam week, the team changes it to three instances, each still with 4 virtual CPUs. Which term describes this change?
choices: Enabling zone redundancy
Scaling out
Scaling up
Changing the size family
questions.why: Adding more instances of the same size is scaling out. Scaling up would make the single instance bigger instead.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm needs to resize each delivery photo when a driver uploads it. Each resize takes about three seconds. Uploads arrive in bursts, with hours of no activity in between. The firm wants to pay as little as possible while nothing is running. Which hosting model fits best?
choices: Azure Kubernetes Service, because a managed container cluster handles bursty traffic
Azure Functions (serverless), because the code runs only when an upload triggers it and is billed per run
Azure Virtual Machines (IaaS), because a rented server gives full control over the resize software
Azure App Service (PaaS) with a large fixed-size plan running all the time
questions.why: Serverless runs short pieces of code only when an event triggers them and bills per run, so the long idle gaps between bursts cost almost nothing.

questions.prompt: A concert-ticketing site runs on one App Service instance sized for its average daily traffic. When a popular show goes on sale, traffic jumps about eightfold and many buyers get slow or failed responses. Which change best addresses the cause?
choices: Move the site to virtual machines, because a server the team manages directly can handle peaks better
Switch to a compute-optimised size that still matches average traffic
Keep one instance and enable zone redundancy so the site survives a datacentre failure
Add autoscale on a metric such as CPU, with a minimum of two instances, so capacity grows automatically during the spike
questions.why: The failure comes from sizing for average load. Autoscale adds instances when a metric such as CPU rises, so the peak gets the capacity it needs.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would turn a workload's requirements into a choice of compute hosting model, size, scaling and availability, and name one tradeoff you accept with each move toward more managed hosting.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start from the requirements, not the service list. First I ask how much control the workload needs: custom OS settings or legacy software push me toward virtual machines, while plain web code with no patching staff points to managed hosting like App Service, and event-triggered short tasks fit serverless Functions. If the code is already in containers, a container host such as Container Apps or AKS makes sense. Next I size each instance for real load, then add autoscale so instances are added at peak and removed when quiet, keeping a minimum for resilience. Finally I spread instances across availability zones to meet the uptime target. The tradeoff is that each step toward more managed hosting removes operational work and idle cost but also removes control: I can't tune the OS, and serverless has run-time and cold-start limits, so long or stateful jobs may not fit.
rubricPoints: Starts from workload requirements such as control, traffic pattern, staffing and uptime.
Distinguishes IaaS, PaaS, containers and serverless by how much the cloud manages.
Sizes instances for real load and uses autoscale with a sensible minimum.
Uses availability zones or redundancy to meet an uptime target.
Names the control-versus-convenience tradeoff, such as lost OS access or serverless limits.

suggested.rationale: This objective is a judgment skill tested through scenarios, so reasoning through exam-style workload situations and defending each component choice builds it best.

lessons.plain: A virtual machine (VM) is a computer made of software that runs on someone else's physical hardware. In Azure you rent one by the hour and get a full operating system you control. You choose its size, its disks, and how many copies run, and you handle patching and the software on it. Recommending a VM-based solution means deciding when that much control is worth the extra upkeep, and then picking the right size, the right resilience option, and the right pricing. It is like leasing an empty house rather than booking a serviced hotel room: you can change anything, but fixing the plumbing is your job.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company runs an old Windows application that needs a special driver installed on the server and must keep running if one Azure datacenter fails. Would you pick a single large VM or several smaller VMs spread across separate datacenters, and why?
lessons.teach:
A VM-based solution is an infrastructure as a service (IaaS) design: Azure provides the hardware and the hypervisor, the software layer that splits one physical server into many VMs, and you manage the operating system and everything above it. Recommend VMs when a workload needs full OS control, such as custom drivers, unsupported legacy software, specific licensing, or a quick lift-and-shift move. Steer away from VMs when a managed platform such as containers or serverless would remove that upkeep.

After choosing VMs, make four decisions. Size comes from VM series, which are families tuned for a purpose: general purpose (B, D), memory optimized (E), compute optimized (F), and GPU (N). Disks are managed disks, which are Azure-run storage volumes in tiers from Standard HDD up to Premium SSD and Ultra Disk for fast input and output.

Resilience is the third decision. An availability set spreads VMs across fault domains (separate racks with their own power and network) and update domains (groups that are rebooted at different times) inside one datacenter. Availability zones are physically separate datacenters within one region, and spreading VMs across them protects against a whole-site failure. Virtual Machine Scale Sets manage a group of identical VMs that can add or remove instances automatically.

Pricing is the fourth decision. Reserved instances give a discount for a one- or three-year commitment. Spot VMs use spare capacity cheaply, but Azure can evict them at short notice. Azure Dedicated Host gives you a whole physical server when compliance requires isolation.

Worked example: the legacy app above needs a driver, so VMs are required. Load doubles at month end, so a scale set is the fit. It must survive a datacenter loss, so the scale set spans three zones. The base load runs on reserved instances.

A common mistake is recommending one large VM for a critical workload. That VM is a single point of failure, so maintenance or a hardware fault takes the whole service offline.

questions.prompt: A logistics company wants to move its warehouse-control program to Azure. The program only installs on an older Windows Server build and needs a vendor-supplied device driver. The architect works through the design. Step 1: the program needs a custom driver, so the team needs full operating system control. That makes virtual machines (an infrastructure as a service design) the right choice. Step 2: the program keeps large datasets in memory, so the architect picks a memory optimized series (E). Step 3: it reads and writes data heavily, so it gets Premium SSD managed disks. Step 4 (missing): the business requires the service to keep running even if one entire datacenter in the region goes offline. Step 5: the load is steady around the clock for at least the next three years, so the VMs use three-year reserved instances. Which choice correctly completes Step 4?
choices: Use one larger VM with Ultra Disk so it has enough headroom to absorb failures
Put the VMs on Azure Dedicated Host so they have a physical server to themselves
Deploy two or more VMs spread across availability zones in the region
Place two or more VMs in an availability set so they sit on separate fault domains and update domains
questions.why: Availability zones are physically separate datacenters within one region, so spreading VMs across them is what protects against losing a whole site; an availability set stays inside a single datacenter.

questions.prompt: An architect places four VMs in an availability set. What is the purpose of the update domains in that set?
choices: They put each VM in a different datacenter so a site-wide outage cannot stop all of them
They divide the VMs into groups that Azure reboots at different times, so planned maintenance never restarts all of them together
They add or remove identical VM instances automatically as load rises and falls
They give each VM its own rack with separate power and networking
questions.why: Update domains are groups that are rebooted at different times, so some VMs stay running during maintenance. Separate racks with their own power describe fault domains, and separate datacenters describe availability zones.

questions.prompt: A small animation studio renders video frames on VMs overnight. Each render job saves its progress and can simply be restarted if it is stopped partway through. The studio has no compliance rules that require server isolation, and its main goal is the lowest possible cost. Which pricing option fits best?
choices: Azure Dedicated Host, so the studio gets a whole physical server to itself
Spot VMs, because they run cheaply on spare capacity and an eviction only means a job restarts
Three-year reserved instances, because a long commitment always gives the deepest discount
Ultra Disk managed disks, so jobs finish faster and cost less
questions.why: Spot VMs are cheap because they use spare capacity. Azure can evict them at short notice, but that is acceptable when interrupted jobs can just be restarted.

questions.prompt: A retailer's order-processing system is business critical. A consultant proposes running it on a single very large D-series VM with Premium SSD disks, arguing that the extra size makes it reliable. What is the main problem with this design?
choices: The single VM is a single point of failure, so a hardware fault or planned maintenance takes the whole service offline
Premium SSD disks cannot be attached to a VM that runs alone
A large VM must use Spot pricing, so Azure could evict it at any time
D-series is memory optimized, so it is the wrong family for order processing
questions.why: No matter how large one VM is, it remains a single point of failure. Critical workloads need multiple VMs spread across fault domains or zones.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you decide whether a workload should run on Azure VMs, and how you would make that VM design resilient and affordable. Name one tradeoff of choosing VMs.
lessons.modelAnswer: I choose VMs when the workload needs control of the operating system: custom drivers, legacy or unsupported software, particular licensing, or a fast lift-and-shift. If a managed platform could run it, I usually prefer that, because with VMs we own patching, security hardening, and backups. That upkeep is the main tradeoff. Next I pick a VM series that matches the workload, for example memory optimized for in-memory work, and a managed disk tier that matches the input/output needs. For resilience I never rely on one VM. An availability set protects against a rack failure or host maintenance inside one datacenter. Availability zones protect against losing a whole datacenter. A scale set adds automatic scaling for variable load. For cost, I use reserved instances for steady baseline load and Spot VMs only for work that can tolerate being interrupted.
rubricPoints: States that VMs fit when full OS control, legacy software, or lift-and-shift is required.
Names the operational burden of IaaS, such as patching and management, as a tradeoff versus PaaS.
Distinguishes availability sets (rack-level, one datacenter) from availability zones (separate datacenters).
Mentions scale sets for automatic scaling of identical VMs.
Matches VM series and disk tier to workload needs.
Uses a pricing option correctly, such as reserved instances for steady load or Spot VMs for interruptible work.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly about weighing requirements against VM size, resilience, and pricing options, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios teaches it best, and no current mission or planned engine covers it directly.

lessons.plain: A container is a sealed lunchbox for software: the program plus everything it needs to run, packed so it behaves the same on any machine. Recommending a container-based solution means choosing where those lunchboxes should run in Azure. The options range from simply running one box on demand, to a managed service that runs many boxes and scales them for you, to a full system you tune yourself. Like picking between a taxi, a bus service and owning a fleet, the right answer depends on how much control the workload needs and how much running effort the team can take on.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team has one small containerized script that runs for ten minutes each night and then stops. Should they set up a full cluster of always-on servers to manage it, or use something simpler? Why?
lessons.teach:
A container is a packaged unit of software that includes the application and its dependencies. It is built from an image, a read-only template, which is stored in a registry, a catalogue of images; Azure Container Registry (ACR) is Azure's private managed registry. An orchestrator is software that starts, restarts, scales and networks many containers; Kubernetes is the most common one.

Azure offers several places to run containers, ordered roughly from least to most control. Azure Container Instances (ACI) runs a single container or small group on demand with no cluster, billed per second; good for short jobs and simple tasks. Azure App Service can run a containerized web app or API with built-in scaling, custom domains and deployment slots. Azure Container Apps is a managed, serverless container platform built on Kubernetes, but it hides the cluster; it scales on HTTP traffic or events, including down to zero, and suits microservices, which are small independent services that make up one application. Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) is managed Kubernetes: Azure runs the control plane, the cluster's brain, while you manage node pools, upgrades, networking and add-ons. Choose it when you need full Kubernetes features, custom operators or fine control.

This works because each step up trades operating effort for control. Worked example: a retailer has twelve microservices, a small team with no Kubernetes skills, traffic spikes during sales, and quiet nights. Step one: many services rules out lone ACI containers. Step two: no Kubernetes skills argues against AKS. Step three: spiky traffic and quiet nights favour scale-to-zero. Recommendation: Container Apps, pulling images from ACR.

A common mistake is defaulting to AKS because it is the most powerful. In a running system, that leaves a small team patching nodes and handling upgrades, raising cost and outage risk without any benefit the workload needed.

questions.prompt: A research lab runs one data-cleaning script packaged as a single container. It runs once each night, finishes in about eight minutes, and then nothing runs until the next night. The lab has no Kubernetes skills and does not host a website. The reasoning so far: Step one: this is one container, not a set of many services, so the lab does not need an orchestrator (software that starts, scales and networks many containers). Step two: [missing]. Step three: it is not a web app or API, so App Service features like custom domains and deployment slots add nothing. Recommendation: Azure Container Instances (ACI), pulling its image (the read-only template the container is built from) from Azure Container Registry (ACR), Azure's private managed catalogue of images. Which statement correctly fills step two?
choices: It needs scale-to-zero, and only Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) can scale a workload down to nothing between runs.
It should run on a permanent cluster whose control plane the lab manages, so the job is always ready to start.
It runs briefly and on demand, so paying per second with no cluster left running in between fits the job.
A short job needs deployment slots so that a new version can be swapped in safely before each nightly run.
questions.why: ACI runs a container on demand with no cluster and bills per second, which matches a short job that sits idle most of the day.

questions.prompt: In Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), Azure's managed Kubernetes offering, which split of responsibilities is correct?
choices: You manage everything, including the control plane; Azure only supplies the hardware.
Azure runs the control plane, the cluster's brain, while you manage node pools, upgrades, networking and add-ons.
Azure manages everything, including node pools and add-ons, and hides the cluster from you.
Azure manages node pools and upgrades, while you run the control plane yourself.
questions.why: AKS is managed Kubernetes in which Azure runs the control plane and the customer keeps responsibility for node pools, upgrades, networking and add-ons.

questions.prompt: An insurance firm has one containerized customer-facing web API. It is not split into microservices (small independent services that make up one application). The firm needs a custom domain, built-in scaling, and the ability to stage a new release in a separate slot before swapping it live. Which Azure service best fits?
choices: Azure Kubernetes Service, because staged releases require full Kubernetes control
Azure Container Instances, because a single container never needs anything more
Azure Container Apps, because every container workload should scale to zero
Azure App Service, running the container as a web app
questions.why: App Service runs a containerized web app or API with built-in scaling, custom domains and deployment slots, which are exactly the stated needs.

questions.prompt: A three-person startup runs a few simple event-driven container services. No one on the team knows Kubernetes and they need no custom operators. They picked Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) because it is the most powerful option. What is the most likely result in the running system?
choices: The services will run faster and cheaper, because more control always lowers cost.
The services cannot pull images from Azure Container Registry when they run on AKS.
The small team must patch nodes and handle upgrades, raising cost and outage risk with no benefit the workload needed.
Nothing changes, because AKS hides the cluster and handles all node work automatically.
questions.why: With AKS the customer manages node pools and upgrades, so choosing it without needing its features adds operating effort, cost and outage risk for no gain.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between Azure Container Instances, Container Apps, App Service and AKS for a containerized workload, and name the main tradeoff behind the choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: All of these run containers, which are packaged apps built from images we keep in a registry like Azure Container Registry. The choice is about control versus operating effort. For a short, simple job, Container Instances runs a container on demand with no cluster and per-second billing. For a single containerized web app or API, App Service gives easy scaling and deployment slots. For a set of microservices that need event- or traffic-based scaling, even down to zero, Container Apps gives Kubernetes-style behaviour without us managing a cluster. AKS is for when we truly need full Kubernetes control, custom tooling or fine networking, and have the skills to manage node pools and upgrades. The tradeoff: more control means more work and more ways to break things, so pick the simplest service that meets the requirements rather than defaulting to AKS.
rubricPoints: Defines a container, image and registry, and mentions Azure Container Registry for storing images.
Matches Container Instances to short or simple on-demand containers without a cluster.
Matches App Service to a single containerized web app or API.
Matches Container Apps to managed, event- or traffic-scaled microservices including scale to zero.
Matches AKS to workloads needing full Kubernetes control and a team able to operate it.
States the tradeoff of control versus operating effort and warns against defaulting to AKS.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine runs container platforms, so reasoning through exam-style workload scenarios to pick the fitting service builds this recommendation skill best.

lessons.plain: Serverless means you hand Azure a small piece of code, or a workflow, and Azure runs it only when something happens, such as a file arriving, a message landing, or a web request. You never pick, patch or size a server, and in the pure pay-per-use form you pay only while the code is running. Think of a taxi instead of owning a car: no parking, insurance or idle cost, but you wait a moment for it to arrive and you cannot keep it all day cheaply. Recommending serverless means spotting workloads that are short, bursty and event-triggered, then picking the right serverless option for them.
lessons.guessPrompt: A small job takes about two seconds and runs whenever a customer uploads a photo, a few hundred times a day and almost never at night. Would you keep a server running all day for it, or pay only for each run? What might you give up by choosing pay-per-run?
lessons.teach:
A serverless solution runs code or workflows in response to events, with the platform handling servers and scaling. Azure Functions is the code-first option: you write a function and attach a trigger, the event that starts it, such as an HTTP request, a new blob (a file in Azure Storage), a queue message or a timer. Azure Logic Apps is the low-code option: you build a workflow visually from connectors, ready-made links to services like email, SharePoint or Salesforce.

The hosting plan decides cost and behaviour. The Consumption plan scales instances out automatically, can scale to zero when idle, and bills per execution, but runs are capped at about ten minutes and an idle app suffers a cold start, a delay while a fresh instance loads. The Premium plan keeps pre-warmed instances so there is no cold start, allows longer runs and can join a virtual network to reach private resources, but you pay for those warm instances even when idle. Flex Consumption is a newer pay-per-use plan that adds virtual network access and optional always-ready instances. A Dedicated (App Service) plan runs functions on servers you already pay for. Durable Functions is an extension for stateful orchestration: it saves progress between steps so a process can wait hours or days without running.

Worked example. Requirement: resize uploaded receipts, bursty by day, idle at night, each resize 20 seconds, no private network needed. Step one: event-triggered and short, so serverless fits. Step two: idle periods and tolerance for a short delay favour Consumption. Step three: 20 seconds is far below the time cap. Recommendation: Functions on Consumption with a blob trigger. If the requirement later adds reaching an on-premises database privately with no startup delay, move to Premium or Flex Consumption.

Common mistake: recommending Consumption for long-running or steady, always-busy work. Runs get cut off at the timeout, and constant load costs more than a fixed plan. Serverless wins for short, spiky, event-driven work; long single tasks belong on containers or VMs, and long multi-step waits belong in Durable Functions or Logic Apps.

questions.prompt: A veterinary clinic chain puts appointment-reminder jobs on a queue. Volume spikes on weekday mornings and is near zero at weekends. Each message takes about 3 seconds to process. The code must read a patient database that is reachable only inside a private virtual network (an isolated network in Azure). A few seconds of startup delay is acceptable, and the clinic wants to pay only for actual use. Step 1: The work is event-triggered and short, so serverless fits. Step 2: The event is a queue message, so use Azure Functions with a queue trigger. Step 3: ??? Step 4: Three seconds is far below any run time cap. Recommendation: Azure Functions on the Flex Consumption plan with a queue trigger. Which reasoning belongs in Step 3?
choices: Private network access rules out plain Consumption, and paying only for use argues against Premium's always-paid warm instances, so Flex Consumption fits.
Durable Functions is needed, because a private database means progress must be saved between steps.
Consumption fits on its own, because pay-per-execution and scale to zero cover every requirement listed.
Premium is required, because any workload that touches a virtual network must keep pre-warmed instances running.
questions.why: Flex Consumption is the pay-per-use plan that adds virtual network access, so it meets the private-database need without paying for idle warm instances as Premium would.

questions.prompt: An events company runs its ticket-lookup API on Azure Functions in the Consumption plan. Traffic stops overnight. Each morning, the first request takes several seconds longer than later requests, which then run quickly. What best explains this?
choices: A cold start: after idling, a fresh instance must load before the first request can run.
The HTTP trigger only checks for new requests every few seconds.
The run time cap of about ten minutes is slowing the first request.
Durable Functions is replaying saved progress before answering.
questions.why: Consumption can scale to zero when idle, so the first request after a quiet period waits while a new instance loads. That delay is called a cold start.

questions.prompt: A developer team at an insurer wants a code-first process. When a claim arrives, the process validates it, then waits for a manager's approval that can take up to five days, then pays out. What should you recommend for the waiting, multi-step part?
choices: A Logic Apps connector to email, because only low-code tools can send notifications.
Durable Functions, which saves progress between steps so the process can wait days without running.
A virtual machine running a loop that checks for approval every minute.
A single function on the Consumption plan that stays running until the approval arrives.
questions.why: Durable Functions adds stateful orchestration that saves progress between steps, so a code-first process can pause for days without consuming run time.

questions.prompt: A media firm proposes Azure Functions on the Consumption plan to transcode training videos. Each video takes about 45 minutes, and jobs arrive steadily all day. What is the main problem with this design?
choices: Each run would be cut off at the roughly ten-minute cap, and constant load is cheaper on a fixed plan, so long single tasks belong on containers or VMs.
Consumption cannot be started by a blob trigger, so new videos would never be detected.
Consumption keeps pre-warmed instances, so the firm would pay for idle capacity overnight.
The only problem is cold starts, which a timer trigger would fix.
questions.why: Consumption caps runs at about ten minutes and suits spiky work, so 45-minute, always-busy jobs would fail and cost more than a fixed option such as containers or VMs.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would recommend Azure Functions on a pay-per-use plan, when you would switch to the Premium plan or Logic Apps instead, and name one limit or tradeoff of going serverless.
lessons.modelAnswer: Serverless fits work that is triggered by events, finishes quickly and arrives in bursts, like resizing an uploaded file or reacting to a queue message. For that I'd pick Azure Functions on the Consumption plan: it scales out on its own, drops to zero when idle, and we pay only per run. The tradeoffs are cold starts, a short delay after idle time, and a cap of roughly ten minutes per run, with no private network access. If we need private network access or no startup delay, I'd move to Premium or Flex Consumption and accept paying for warm instances. If the job is mostly wiring services together, or business staff need to read the flow, Logic Apps with connectors suits better. For processes that wait days, like approvals, I'd use Durable Functions. Long single compute tasks or steady constant load usually belong on containers or VMs instead.
rubricPoints: Defines serverless as event-triggered code or workflow where the platform manages servers and scaling.
Matches short, bursty, event-driven work to Functions on a pay-per-use Consumption plan.
Names cold start and the execution time cap as Consumption limits.
Explains when Premium or Flex Consumption is needed, such as virtual network access or no cold start, and its idle cost.
Distinguishes Logic Apps for low-code connector workflows and Durable Functions for long-waiting stateful processes.
Notes that long single tasks or constant heavy load suit containers or VMs better.

suggested.rationale: The skill is choosing the right serverless option and hosting plan from stated requirements, which is best practised by reasoning through exam-style scenarios, reinforced by the existing serverless incident missions.

lessons.plain: Batch processing means running a large amount of work that does not need an instant answer, such as rendering movie frames, running financial risk models, or converting thousands of videos. You usually split it into many small independent pieces and run them in parallel on many machines, then shut the machines down. Think of a print shop with a big overnight order: the manager hands pages to as many printers as the deadline needs, then switches them off. On Azure, choosing a compute solution for batch means picking the service that acts as that manager and supplies the right number and kind of machines at a sensible cost.
lessons.guessPrompt: You must render 10,000 animation frames that each take about 10 minutes of CPU time, and the results are due tomorrow morning. Would you run them one after another on one big server, or spread them across many machines at once? What would you want to happen to those machines when the job finishes?
lessons.teach:
A batch workload is a large job made of many tasks, where a task is one independent unit of work, such as one frame or one file. Azure Batch is a managed job scheduler: you define a pool, which is a group of virtual machines (VMs, rented computers) called compute nodes, and a job, which is a collection of tasks. Batch queues the tasks, assigns them to idle nodes, retries failed ones, and can grow or shrink the pool with an autoscale formula, so you pay for machines only while work exists. Pools can use Spot VMs, which are spare capacity sold at a deep discount that Azure may reclaim at short notice.

Why it works: independent tasks need no coordination, so doubling the nodes roughly halves the time. Batch also suits high-performance computing (HPC), meaning tightly coupled jobs that need fast networking between nodes.

Worked example: 10,000 frames at 10 minutes each is 100,000 compute-minutes. With 100 single-task nodes, that is about 1,000 minutes, roughly 17 hours, which misses a 10-hour deadline. With 500 nodes it is about 200 minutes, roughly 3.3 hours. Using Spot nodes cuts cost; because frames are independent, an evicted task is simply requeued and rerun.

Alternatives matter. Azure Functions (serverless code triggered by events) fits short, lightweight tasks but has execution time limits, so it is a poor fit for long CPU-heavy work. Azure Container Apps jobs fit containerized tasks that run on a schedule or event and then stop. Plain VM scale sets work if you want to build your own scheduler, but then you own the queueing and retry logic that Batch gives you.

Common mistake: picking Spot VMs for long tasks without checkpointing, which means saving progress partway through. In a running system, evictions then restart hours-long tasks from zero, so costs and finish times climb instead of falling. Recommend Batch for large parallel or HPC jobs, and match the VM size and pricing model to task length and deadline.

questions.prompt:
A genomics lab must process 6,000 DNA samples. Each sample is an independent task that takes 20 minutes on one single-task compute node, and the whole run must finish within 10 hours. The architect works it through:
Step 1: Total work = 6,000 samples x 20 minutes = 120,000 compute-minutes.
Step 2: Deadline in minutes = 10 hours x 60 = 600 minutes.
Step 3: ???
Step 4: Recommend an Azure Batch pool of at least that size, with an autoscale formula so the pool shrinks to zero once the task queue is empty.
Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Minimum nodes = 6,000, because Batch must give every task its own dedicated node for the whole run
Minimum nodes = 600 / 20 = 30, because each node can finish 30 samples within the deadline
Minimum nodes = 120,000 / 600 = 200, dividing the total work by the deadline in minutes
Minimum nodes = 120,000 / 10 = 12,000, dividing the total work by the deadline in hours
questions.why: Because the tasks are independent, the run time is roughly total compute-minutes divided by the node count, so 120,000 compute-minutes spread over 200 nodes takes about 600 minutes, which meets the 10-hour deadline.

questions.prompt: In Azure Batch, what is a pool?
choices: A formula that decides when Spot capacity is reclaimed by Azure
A group of virtual machines, called compute nodes, that run the tasks Batch assigns to them
A collection of tasks that together make up one large job
A single independent unit of work, such as one file or one frame
questions.why: A pool is the set of rented machines (compute nodes) that do the work; a job is the collection of tasks, and a task is one unit of work.

questions.prompt: A climate research group runs 300 independent simulation tasks. Each task takes about 8 hours and saves no progress partway through. To cut costs, they move the whole pool to Spot VMs. What is the most likely result in the running system?
choices: Batch refuses to schedule tasks longer than one hour on Spot VMs
Nothing changes, because Spot VMs are never reclaimed while a task is running
Costs fall sharply with no effect on finish time, because Batch moves a running task to another node without losing progress
When Azure reclaims Spot nodes, interrupted tasks restart from zero, so costs and finish times can climb instead of falling
questions.why: Without checkpointing, which means saving progress partway through, every eviction throws away hours of work, so the rerun tasks cost more and finish later.

questions.prompt: An engineering firm must run 2,000 independent stress simulations. Each one is CPU-heavy and runs for about 3 hours. The software is not containerized, and the team does not want to write its own queueing or retry logic. Which compute solution should you recommend?
choices: Azure Batch, because it is a managed scheduler that queues tasks, retries failures and autoscales the pool of nodes
Run all simulations one after another on a single large VM to avoid scheduling complexity
Plain VM scale sets, because they give full control over the machines
Azure Functions, because serverless code scales out automatically for any workload
questions.why: Azure Batch handles queueing, retries and pool autoscaling for large parallel jobs, while Functions has execution time limits that are a poor fit for long CPU-heavy work, and scale sets would make the team build its own scheduler.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would recommend Azure Batch for a batch workload instead of Azure Functions or Container Apps jobs, and name one tradeoff of running the pool on Spot VMs.
lessons.modelAnswer: Batch work is a big job split into independent tasks that can run in parallel. Azure Batch is a managed scheduler: we define a pool of VMs and a job of tasks, and it hands tasks to idle nodes, retries failures and autoscales the pool so we only pay while there is work. I would pick it for large, long-running, CPU-heavy or HPC jobs like rendering or simulations. Functions suits short event-triggered tasks because of execution time limits, and Container Apps jobs suit containerized tasks that run on a schedule and stop. For cost we can run the pool on Spot VMs, which are much cheaper, but Azure can reclaim them at short notice. That is fine when tasks are short or checkpoint their progress, but long tasks without checkpoints restart from zero after eviction, which can blow the deadline and erase the savings.
rubricPoints: Defines batch work as many independent tasks that can run in parallel.
Describes Azure Batch as a managed scheduler over a pool of VMs with retries and autoscaling.
Recommends Batch for large, long-running or HPC jobs and Functions or Container Apps jobs for short or containerized tasks.
Explains that Spot VMs are cheap but can be evicted.
Names checkpointing or short tasks as the way to make Spot evictions tolerable.

suggested.rationale: The exam skill is weighing task length, scale, deadline and cost to choose between Batch, serverless and container options, which is best practised by reasoning through scenario questions.

lessons.plain: A messaging architecture lets parts of a system talk by leaving messages with a go-between instead of calling each other directly. Think of a restaurant ticket rail: waiters pin orders up, and cooks take them when ready. If the kitchen is slammed, tickets wait on the rail instead of getting lost, and waiters keep serving. In Azure, the main choice is between a simple, cheap queue (Queue Storage) and a feature-rich business message broker (Service Bus). Your job is to read the requirements and pick the right one. Those requirements include ordering, failure handling, and how many receivers need each message.
lessons.guessPrompt: An order service hands each order to a billing service. Billing goes offline for an hour. What happens to the orders if the order service calls billing directly? What changes if it drops each order into a queue that billing reads later?
lessons.teach:
A messaging architecture is a design where a producer (the sender) puts messages into a broker, and a consumer (the receiver) takes them out later. A broker is a managed middleman that stores messages. Because neither side waits for the other, the producer keeps working when the consumer is slow or down, and traffic spikes simply become a backlog. This is called queue-based load leveling.

Azure has two main brokers. Azure Queue Storage is a basic queue inside a storage account. It is cheap, holds small messages (up to 64 KB) and can hold very large backlogs, but it makes no ordering promise. Azure Service Bus is an enterprise broker with many more features. Queues give each message to one consumer. Topics with subscriptions give every subscriber its own copy, a pattern called publish-subscribe. Sessions keep related messages in first-in-first-out order. A dead-letter queue is a holding area for messages that keep failing. Service Bus also offers duplicate detection, transactions and larger messages. Event Hubs (high-volume telemetry streaming) and Event Grid (notifications that something happened) carry events rather than work commands, and belong to event-driven design.

Worked example: a retailer has three needs. Orders must be handled in sequence per customer, failed orders must be kept for review, and both billing and shipping must receive every order. Step 1: each order is work that must be done, so use a message broker. Step 2: per-customer ordering requires Service Bus sessions, because Queue Storage cannot guarantee order. Step 3: keeping failed orders points to the dead-letter queue. Step 4: two receivers each need a copy, so use a topic with two subscriptions. The recommendation is a Service Bus topic, on the Premium tier if the retailer needs isolated, predictable performance.

Common mistake: choosing Queue Storage when ordering or dead-lettering is required. In production, one malformed message (a poison message) gets retried endlessly, or orders run out of sequence. Brokers may deliver a message more than once, so consumers must be idempotent: handling the same message twice must give the same result.

questions.prompt: A car insurer is designing how its web portal hands insurance claims to a back-end claims processor. Its requirements: claims for the same policy must be processed in the order they were submitted, a customer who double-clicks Submit must not create two claims, and only one processor should handle each claim. The design is mostly worked out. Step 1: each claim is work that must be done, not just a notice that something happened, so a message broker fits. Step 2: [MISSING]. Step 3: double submissions call for Service Bus duplicate detection, and the processor should still be idempotent (handling the same message twice gives the same result) because brokers can deliver a message more than once. Step 4: each claim needs exactly one receiver, so a Service Bus queue fits rather than a topic. Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: Send each claim through Event Grid, because it reacts instantly when a claim is created and so keeps claims in order.
Use Service Bus sessions keyed on the policy number, because sessions keep related messages in first-in-first-out order.
Turn on the Service Bus dead-letter queue, because it holds claims until earlier claims for the same policy finish.
Use Azure Queue Storage and have the processor sort claims by their submission time, since it holds large backlogs cheaply.
questions.why: Per-policy ordering needs related messages kept first-in-first-out, which Service Bus sessions provide and Queue Storage cannot guarantee.

questions.prompt: A ticketing website gets 50 times its normal traffic for ten minutes when a popular concert goes on sale. The order-processing service behind it can only handle a steady rate. The architect places a broker between the website and the processor so the website keeps accepting orders and the surge turns into a backlog the processor works through. What is this approach called?
choices: Queue-based load leveling
Dead-lettering
Publish-subscribe
Duplicate detection
questions.why: Putting a broker between producer and consumer so spikes become a backlog the consumer drains at its own pace is queue-based load leveling.

questions.prompt: A photo-sharing startup needs to send resize jobs from its upload service to a pool of workers. Each job message is about 2 KB, the backlog can reach millions of jobs during busy periods, order does not matter, each job needs only one worker, and keeping cost as low as possible is the top priority. Which broker should the architect recommend?
choices: Azure Event Hubs, because it handles high-volume streams
Azure Service Bus Premium tier with a topic and one subscription per worker
Azure Queue Storage, a basic low-cost queue in a storage account
Azure Service Bus with sessions to keep jobs in sequence
questions.why: Small messages, very large backlogs, no ordering need and lowest cost match Azure Queue Storage, so Service Bus features would add cost without adding value.

questions.prompt: A payroll company uses a broker to send payment instructions to a worker that transfers money to employees. After a brief network fault, some employees are paid twice, because the broker delivered the same message to the worker a second time. Which design change most directly prevents this harm?
choices: Switch from a Service Bus queue to a topic with subscriptions so each message has its own copy
Send the payments through Event Grid so each one becomes a notification instead
Move the messages to Azure Queue Storage, which delivers each message exactly once
Make the worker idempotent so handling the same payment message twice gives the same result
questions.why: Brokers may deliver a message more than once, so the consumer must be idempotent: processing a repeated payment message must not pay the employee again.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between Azure Queue Storage and Azure Service Bus for a new workload. Name one tradeoff of each choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both are managed brokers. A producer drops messages in and a consumer pulls them out later, so the two sides are decoupled and spikes become a backlog instead of an outage. I start from the requirements. If we just need a cheap queue for background jobs, with small messages, a possibly huge backlog and no ordering needs, Queue Storage fits and costs less. The tradeoff is that it has no ordering guarantee, no built-in publish-subscribe and only basic failure handling. If we need first-in-first-out per group (sessions), a dead-letter queue for failing messages, duplicate detection, transactions, or several subscribers each getting a copy (topics), I recommend Service Bus. The tradeoff there is higher cost and more to configure. Either way, delivery can repeat, so our consumers must be idempotent.
rubricPoints: Defines a broker as a middleman that decouples producers from consumers and absorbs load spikes.
Says Queue Storage is cheap and simple, with small messages and large backlogs but no ordering guarantee.
Names Service Bus features that drive the choice: sessions, dead-letter queue, topics and subscriptions, duplicate detection.
Links each requirement, such as ordering, failure retention or multiple receivers, to a specific feature.
States a tradeoff such as cost and complexity versus missing features.
Notes that consumers should be idempotent because messages can be delivered more than once.

suggested.rationale: A messaging engine would let the learner configure queues, topics, sessions and dead-lettering, and watch how each choice behaves under failures and spikes.

lessons.plain: An event-driven architecture is a way of building software where parts of a system react to things that have happened, instead of constantly asking each other for updates. When something notable occurs, like a file being uploaded or an order being placed, one part announces it, and any interested parts respond on their own. Think of a doorbell. You do not walk to the door every minute to check for visitors. The bell rings once, and whoever cares answers it. The sender does not need to know who is listening, so new listeners can be added without changing the sender.
lessons.guessPrompt: A photo-sharing app needs three things to happen whenever a user uploads a picture: make a thumbnail, scan it for harmful content, and update a search index. Would you have the upload code call all three jobs directly, or announce 'a photo arrived' and let each job react? What could go wrong with each choice?
lessons.teach:
An event is a small, factual notice that something happened, such as 'blob created' or 'order placed'. A publisher (also called a producer) emits the event. A subscriber (or consumer) reacts to it. In between sits a broker, a service that receives events and hands them on, so publisher and subscriber never talk directly. This separation is called loose coupling. It means one side can change, scale, or fail without breaking the other, and fan-out (one event reaching many subscribers) needs no new code in the publisher.

On Azure, two services carry most event-driven designs. Azure Event Grid is a managed event router. It pushes discrete events, delivering each one to subscriber endpoints such as Azure Functions or webhooks. It can filter by event type and retry failed deliveries. Azure Event Hubs is a managed streaming ingestion service built for millions of events per second, such as telemetry. It splits the stream into partitions, which are ordered lanes that allow parallel reading. It keeps data for a retention period, and consumer groups let separate readers move through the same stream at their own pace.

Worked example: a user uploads a photo to Blob Storage. First, storage publishes a 'blob created' event to Event Grid. Second, Event Grid matches two subscriptions, one filtered to image files. Third, it pushes the event to a thumbnail function and a content-scan function at the same time. Fourth, if the scan function is down, Event Grid retries delivery. Now suppose 20,000 delivery vans each send their position every few seconds. That is a continuous high-volume stream, so Event Hubs ingests it and an analytics reader consumes the partitions.

A common mistake is treating events and commands as the same thing. A command is an instruction that must be processed exactly once and often in order, such as 'charge this card'. That job belongs to a message queue like Azure Service Bus, which is covered in the messaging objective. If you force commands through an event router, a running system can drop or duplicate work during failures, and nothing can easily stop that.

questions.prompt: A bookshop chain wants its loyalty system, its warehouse and its sales dashboard to react whenever a customer finishes checkout. The architect traces the design. Step 1: the checkout service publishes one 'order placed' event to Azure Event Grid, a managed event router. Step 2: Event Grid finds three matching subscriptions: a loyalty-points function, a warehouse webhook and a dashboard function. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the warehouse webhook is briefly offline, so Event Grid retries delivery to it while the other two subscribers carry on. Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: The checkout service sends three separate copies of the event, one addressed to each subscriber, so that every one of them receives it.
Each subscriber polls the checkout service every few seconds and asks it directly whether a new order has been placed.
Event Grid pushes the single event out to all three subscriber endpoints, and the checkout service needs no extra code for this fan-out.
Event Grid writes the event into ordered partitions, and each subscriber uses its own consumer group to read the stream later.
questions.why: Event Grid is a broker that pushes each event to every matching subscription, so the publisher emits once and fan-out needs no new publisher code.

questions.prompt: A travel company puts a broker between its booking service (the publisher) and its email service (the subscriber), so the two never talk to each other directly. What is the main benefit of this loose coupling?
choices: The booking service can confirm that the email was actually delivered before it finishes.
Either side can change, scale or fail without breaking the other, and adding subscribers needs no publisher changes.
The broker turns events into commands, so subscribers know exactly what work to do.
Every event is guaranteed to be processed exactly once and in the order it was sent.
questions.why: Loose coupling means the publisher and subscriber are separated by the broker, so each can change, scale or fail independently and fan-out needs no new publisher code.

questions.prompt: An energy firm runs 6,000 wind turbines, each sending sensor readings every second. A forecasting team and a maintenance team must each read the same full stream at their own pace, and the data must be kept for a while after it arrives. Which Azure service fits best?
choices: Azure Service Bus, because every reading is an instruction that must be processed exactly once.
A webhook on each team's server that the turbines call directly, avoiding any broker.
Azure Event Hubs, a managed streaming ingestion service with partitions, a retention period and consumer groups.
Azure Event Grid, because it pushes each discrete event to subscriber endpoints and retries failures.
questions.why: A continuous high-volume telemetry stream read independently by two teams fits Event Hubs, whose partitions, retention and consumer groups support exactly that.

questions.prompt: A payroll team plans to send 'pay employee 4471 this amount' notices through Azure Event Grid to a payment function. What is the main risk in this design?
choices: Event Grid only accepts events from Blob Storage, so the payroll system could not publish to it.
Event Grid cannot filter by event type, so the payment function would receive every other event too.
These are commands that must run exactly once, so during failures the system could drop or duplicate payments; a message queue such as Azure Service Bus fits better.
Nothing is wrong, because Event Grid retries failed deliveries, which guarantees each payment happens exactly once.
questions.why: A 'pay this employee' notice is a command, not an event, and forcing commands through an event router risks dropped or duplicated work, so it belongs in a message queue like Service Bus.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would recommend Event Grid versus Event Hubs for an event-driven design, and name one limit or tradeoff of going event-driven at all.
lessons.modelAnswer: Event-driven means components react to notices that something happened, through a broker, so the publisher does not know or care who is listening. That loose coupling lets us add subscribers, scale them, or take them down without touching the publisher. I would pick Event Grid when we have discrete reactive events, like a blob being created or a resource changing, and want them pushed to a few handlers with filtering and retries. I would pick Event Hubs when we have a high-volume stream such as device telemetry. It partitions the data for parallel reads, keeps it for a retention window, and lets several consumer groups replay it independently. The tradeoff is that the flow becomes harder to trace and test, and delivery can repeat, so handlers must be safe to run twice. If the work is really a command that must be processed exactly once and in order, like charging a card, I would use a message queue such as Service Bus instead.
rubricPoints: Defines an event as a notice of something that happened, sent through a broker that decouples publisher and subscriber.
Recommends Event Grid for discrete, reactive events pushed to handlers with filtering and fan-out.
Recommends Event Hubs for high-volume streaming ingestion with partitions, retention and consumer groups.
Distinguishes events from commands that need a message queue such as Service Bus.
Names a tradeoff such as harder tracing, eventual consistency, or duplicate delivery requiring idempotent handlers.

suggested.rationale: The exam skill is matching a scenario's event volume and delivery needs to Event Grid, Event Hubs, or a queue, which is best practised by reasoning through exam-style situations after the teaching.

lessons.plain: API integration means giving many different apps and partners one tidy, controlled way to call your back-end services. Azure's main answer is Azure API Management, a managed API gateway: a front door that sits between callers and your services. Think of a hotel reception desk. Guests never wander into the kitchen or laundry. They ask at the desk, which checks who they are, limits how often they can ask, and passes the request to the right department. Departments can be rebuilt behind the scenes without guests noticing, because the desk's address and manners stay the same.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company has three separate back-end services, and 40 partner companies want to call them. Would you give each partner the direct address of every service, or put something in front of them? What problems could a single front door solve?
lessons.teach:
An API (application programming interface) is a defined way for one program to request work from another, usually over HTTPS. Azure API Management (APIM) is a managed API gateway: one public endpoint that receives calls, applies rules, and forwards each call to the right backend (the service that does the real work). It also includes a developer portal, a website where callers read documentation and get keys. APIM groups APIs into products, which are bundles a caller subscribes to. A subscription key is the secret a caller sends to prove which subscription it is using. Policies are rules that run on each request or response, such as rate limiting (capping calls per minute), response caching, header rewriting, or validating a token.

This works because cross-cutting concerns live in one place, so backends stay simple and can change without breaking callers. Versioning lets v1 and v2 of an API run side by side.

Worked example: partners need one address, a cap of 100 calls per minute each, and access to an order service on App Service plus an on-premises inventory system. A partner calls the APIM endpoint with its key. APIM checks the key, then applies the rate-limit policy. Next it checks the cache. If the cache has nothing, APIM routes the call. Order calls go to App Service. Inventory calls travel over a private network link into the on-premises system. On-premises reach needs a tier that can join a virtual network, typically Premium. A self-hosted gateway, which runs inside your own data centre, also works. Consumption is a serverless, pay-per-call tier and suits light or spiky public traffic. Developer has no uptime agreement, so it is not for production.

Common mistake: recommending a load balancer such as Application Gateway or Front Door for this. Those spread traffic and can block attacks, but they do not manage API keys, products or a developer portal. In a running system, the gateway sits in every call path. Size it and make it redundant, or it becomes a single point of failure.

questions.prompt: A city transit agency wants to let third-party app makers read live bus arrival times. The arrivals service runs on Azure Functions and is reachable over the public internet. Requirements: one public address, a key for each app maker, published documentation, and a cap of 30 calls per minute per app maker. Traffic is light most of the day with sharp spikes at rush hour. The architect's design: Step 1, place Azure API Management (a managed API gateway) in front of the Functions backend so every call goes to one endpoint. Step 2, bundle the arrivals API into a product called Transit Data; app makers sign up through the developer portal and receive a subscription key. Step 3: MISSING. Step 4, choose the Consumption tier, because the backend is public and the traffic is light and spiky. Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Add code to the Functions backend so that it counts each app maker's calls and rejects any extra ones
Put Azure Front Door in front of API Management to enforce the 30-calls-per-minute cap for each app maker
Move to the Developer tier so the cap can be tested and enforced on live traffic
Attach a rate-limit policy in API Management that caps each subscription at 30 calls per minute
questions.why: A rate-limit policy runs in the gateway on every request, so the per-caller cap is enforced in one place and the backend stays simple.

questions.prompt: In Azure API Management, what is a product?
choices: A rule that runs on each request, such as caching a response or rewriting a header
A separate version of an API, such as v2, that runs alongside v1
The backend service, such as an App Service app, that does the real work behind an API
A bundle of APIs that a caller subscribes to, receiving a subscription key for it
questions.why: APIM groups APIs into products, and a caller subscribes to a product and then uses a subscription key to prove which subscription it is using.

questions.prompt: An insurance firm needs a production API gateway with a service-level uptime agreement. The gateway must forward claims calls privately to a policy database system that runs in the firm's own data centre, through a virtual network (a private network in Azure). The gateway must be hosted by Azure, so a self-hosted gateway is ruled out. Which API Management tier fits?
choices: Developer, because it supports every feature needed for testing
Azure Application Gateway, because it can spread traffic and block attacks
Premium, because it can join a virtual network to reach on-premises systems
Consumption, because its serverless, pay-per-call model lowers cost
questions.why: Reaching on-premises systems needs a tier that can join a virtual network, typically Premium; Developer has no uptime agreement, and Application Gateway is a load balancer, not an API Management tier.

questions.prompt: A retailer routes all supplier API traffic through a single API Management gateway instance. One morning that instance fails, and every supplier call fails, even though all backend services are healthy. What design lesson does this show?
choices: The gateway sits in every call path, so it must be sized and made redundant to avoid a single point of failure
A response-caching policy would have kept all calls working while the gateway was down
Suppliers should call the backends directly, because a gateway adds no value for partner traffic
Application Gateway should replace API Management, because it manages keys more reliably
questions.why: Because every request passes through the gateway, an unsized, non-redundant gateway becomes a single point of failure for the whole system.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why you would put Azure API Management in front of several backend services instead of exposing them directly, and name one limit or tradeoff of doing so.
lessons.modelAnswer: API Management is a managed gateway that gives every caller one stable address. Instead of each backend handling keys, throttling and documentation its own way, the gateway does it once. It checks the subscription key and applies policies like rate limits, caching or token checks. Then it routes the call to the right backend, whether that is App Service, Functions or an on-premises system. Callers subscribe to products and learn the APIs through the developer portal. Versioning lets us change a backend without breaking partners. The tradeoff is that the gateway now sits in every request. It adds a small amount of latency and cost, and if it is undersized or not redundant, it can take everything down. Tier choice also matters. Consumption is cheap per call but cannot join a private network, and reaching on-premises usually needs Premium or a self-hosted gateway.
rubricPoints: Defines API Management as a gateway giving one endpoint in front of several backends.
Names central concerns it handles such as keys, rate limits, caching or versioning.
Mentions products, subscriptions or the developer portal for onboarding callers.
Links tier choice to requirements such as private network or on-premises access.
States a tradeoff such as added latency, cost or the gateway becoming a single point of failure.
Distinguishes it from load balancers like Application Gateway or Front Door.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine exercises an API gateway, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios that pick a tier and features from stated requirements builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: A cache is a small, very fast store that keeps copies of data an application asks for often, so it does not have to go back to the slower original source every time. Think of a notepad by the phone with the numbers you dial most, instead of searching the full directory each call. In Azure, the main managed cache for application data is Azure Cache for Redis, an in-memory key-value store that Microsoft runs for you. For files such as images and scripts, a content delivery network keeps copies close to users. Recommending a cache means choosing what to cache, where, for how long, and which tier fits.
lessons.guessPrompt: An online shop's product pages load slowly because every visit queries the database, yet product details change only a few times a day. Where would you keep a copy of those details so pages load faster, and what risk does keeping a copy create?
lessons.teach:
A cache hit means the data was found in the cache; a cache miss means it was not and must be fetched from the source, such as a database. A TTL (time to live) is how long a cached item stays before it expires. Eviction is the cache discarding items when memory fills up.

The most common design is cache-aside: the application checks the cache first; on a miss it reads the database, stores the result in the cache with a TTL, then returns it. It works because memory reads take well under a millisecond while database queries take far longer, and most reads repeat the same popular items.

Azure Cache for Redis is a managed in-memory key-value store. Its tiers matter for the exam: Basic is a single node with no SLA (a service-level agreement, Microsoft's uptime commitment), suited to dev and test; Standard adds a replica for failover and an SLA; Premium adds clustering (splitting data across nodes for size and throughput), data persistence, private virtual network placement and geo-replication; Enterprise tiers add Redis Enterprise modules and active geo-replication. For static files, Azure Front Door or Azure CDN caches content at edge locations near users. Redis is also a good store for user sessions shared across many web servers.

Worked example: a catalog API serves 5,000 reads per second from one database. Step one, identify read-heavy, rarely changing data: product details. Step two, choose cache-aside with a 10-minute TTL. Step three, it is production and needs failover, so pick Standard or higher, not Basic. Step four, product images go to Front Door. Database load drops sharply.

A common mistake is treating the cache as the only copy of important data, or caching data that must always be current, such as account balances. Another is letting many popular keys expire at once: when the cache empties, every request hits the database together, a cache stampede that can overload it and slow the whole system.

questions.prompt: A regional transit company runs a journey-planner app that receives about 3,000 timetable lookups per second against one SQL database. Security policy says the cache must sit inside the company's private virtual network, and the team wants cached data persisted to disk so a restart does not start from empty. Step 1: Identify read-heavy, rarely changing data. Route timetables change only once a week. Step 2: Use cache-aside with a 30-minute TTL (time to live, how long an item stays before it expires). Step 3: MISSING. Choose the lowest Azure Cache for Redis tier that meets the network and persistence requirements. Step 4: Send the static route-map images to an edge cache (Azure Front Door or Azure CDN). Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Premium tier, because it is the lowest tier that offers private virtual network placement and data persistence.
Skip Redis and put the timetables in Front Door, because edge caching already handles every kind of data.
Basic tier, because it is the cheapest single-node cache and the data rarely changes.
Standard tier, because it adds a replica for failover and comes with an SLA.
questions.why: Premium is the first tier that adds private virtual network placement and data persistence, while Basic and Standard lack both, and Front Door is meant for static files rather than application data lookups.

questions.prompt: A recipe website uses the cache-aside pattern with Azure Cache for Redis. A visitor requests a recipe that is not currently in the cache, which is a cache miss. What should the application do next?
choices: Return an error to the visitor and wait for the cache to load the recipe by itself.
Read the recipe from the database, store it in the cache with a TTL, then return it to the visitor.
Evict the least popular recipes from the cache so there is room, then ask the visitor to try again.
Write the recipe from the cache back to the database, then return it to the visitor.
questions.why: In cache-aside, a miss means the application fetches the item from the source, saves it in the cache with an expiry, and returns it, so later reads of that item become fast cache hits.

questions.prompt: An online learning platform loads its 50,000 most popular course pages into Redis at 02:00 each night, all with the same 24-hour TTL. Every night at exactly 02:00 the database CPU spikes to 100% and the whole site slows down for several minutes. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Eviction, because the cache memory fills up when the pages are loaded.
The Basic tier has no SLA, so the cache goes offline at the same time every night.
Too many cache hits, because the popular pages are read so often from memory.
A cache stampede, because many popular keys expire at once and every request falls through to the database together.
questions.why: When many popular keys share the same expiry time, they all disappear together, and the flood of cache misses hits the database at once, which is a cache stampede.

questions.prompt: A concert ticketing company wants to add Azure Cache for Redis using cache-aside with a 15-minute TTL. Which piece of data is the worst candidate to serve from that cache?
choices: The number of seats still available, checked at the final purchase step, which must always be exact.
Venue descriptions and seating chart layouts.
The list of genres shown in the site's navigation menu.
Artist biography pages that are edited a few times a year.
questions.why: Data that must always be current should not be served from a cache with a 15-minute TTL, because a stale seat count could let customers buy seats that are already sold.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would add caching to a read-heavy web application in Azure, which service and tier you would pick, and one limit or tradeoff they must accept.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd use the cache-aside pattern with Azure Cache for Redis, a managed in-memory key-value store. The app checks Redis first; on a miss it reads the database, writes the result to Redis with a TTL, and returns it. That serves repeated reads from memory and takes load off the database. For production I'd pick Standard at minimum so there's a replica and an SLA; Premium if we need clustering, persistence, private network placement or geo-replication. Static images and scripts go to Front Door or a CDN at the edge. The tradeoff is staleness: users can see data up to one TTL old, so I wouldn't cache values that must be exact, like balances. The cache is also not the system of record, and if many keys expire together we risk a stampede on the database, so I'd stagger TTLs.
rubricPoints: Defines a cache as a fast copy of frequently read data in front of a slower source.
Describes cache-aside: check cache, on miss read source and populate with a TTL.
Names Azure Cache for Redis and matches tier to need, avoiding Basic for production.
Mentions a CDN or Front Door for static content at the edge.
States the staleness tradeoff and that the cache is not the system of record.
Notes the stampede risk when many entries expire or the cache empties.

suggested.rationale: Diagnosing a real cache stampede makes the learner see why TTLs, cache-aside behavior and cache sizing matter when recommending a caching design.

lessons.plain: Application configuration management means keeping an app's settings, such as connection addresses, timeouts, and on/off switches for features, in one shared place outside the code, rather than baked into each server or each copy of the app. Think of a restaurant chain that posts today's menu on one central board that every branch reads, instead of reprinting menus at each location. Change the board once and every branch follows. In Azure, the managed service for this is Azure App Configuration. It stores settings and feature switches centrally, and it works alongside a separate locked safe, Azure Key Vault, which holds the secrets.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your app runs on 20 servers, and each server keeps its own copy of a settings file. You need to switch off a buggy new feature right now. What makes this slow and risky, and what would you want instead?
lessons.teach:
Azure App Configuration is a managed central store for application settings. A key-value is one setting: a name such as Map:RefreshSeconds paired with a value such as 30. A label is a tag on a key-value that lets the same key carry different values, for example one value labelled Dev and another labelled Prod. A feature flag is a stored on/off switch, optionally with rules such as 'on for 10% of users', that the code checks before running a feature. A Key Vault reference is a pointer stored in App Configuration that tells the app to fetch the real secret from Azure Key Vault, the dedicated managed secret store. A managed identity is an Azure-issued identity for the app, so it can authenticate to both stores without any password in code.

This design works because it separates code from settings and settings from secrets. One change in one place reaches every instance, and each store can have its own access control.

Worked example: a fleet-tracking API runs on 20 App Service instances. (1) Shared settings are stored as key-values labelled Prod and Dev, and each environment loads only its own label. (2) The database password stays in Key Vault, and App Configuration holds only a reference to it. (3) The app signs in with a managed identity, which has read access to both stores. (4) A new map view sits behind a feature flag. When it misbehaves, an operator turns the flag off once. (5) The apps watch a sentinel key, a single key that is changed last, and reload all their settings when it changes. Within the refresh interval, all 20 instances stop showing the feature, with no redeployment.

A common mistake is storing secrets as plain key-values in App Configuration. They then sit outside Key Vault's secret-specific protections and auditing, and anyone who can read settings can read the secrets. A second mistake is assuming changes apply instantly. Without a refresh setup, apps keep stale values until they restart, and having every instance poll every key too often can hit request limits.

For exam scenarios, the higher tiers add features such as more requests, replicas in other regions, and private networking. Recommend App Configuration plus Key Vault whenever many instances or services must share settings and toggle features safely.

questions.prompt: A hospital appointment-booking service runs on 8 virtual machines, with a Test environment and a Live environment. The team designs its configuration like this. First, shared settings such as Booking:MaxSlotsPerDay = 40 are stored in Azure App Configuration (a managed central settings store) as key-values, each tagged with a label of Test or Live, and each environment loads only its own label. Second, the API key for the SMS text-message provider is handled in a way that is MISSING here. Third, the app signs in with a managed identity (an Azure-issued identity, so no password sits in code) that has read access to App Configuration and Azure Key Vault. Fourth, a new appointment-reminder feature sits behind a feature flag, a stored on/off switch. Fifth, the apps watch one sentinel key, changed last, and reload their settings when it changes. Which choice correctly fills the missing second step?
choices: Put the SMS API key in a local settings file on each of the 8 virtual machines
Store the SMS API key as a feature flag so an operator can switch it off
Store the SMS API key as a plain key-value labelled Live in App Configuration, so it sits alongside the other settings
Keep the SMS API key in Key Vault, and store only a Key Vault reference to it in App Configuration
